title: Modelling a Cell Type
intro: A computational model of a cell type is a neuron model plus a parameter set that makes it behave like recordings from that type. The same type can be modelled at very different levels of detail, from a reconstructed morphology with a dozen ion channels to a two-variable equation tuned to reproduce the spike pattern. This page lays out the levels, how parameters are fitted, and where to find published models.

items: Detailed multi-compartment, conductance-based models: the real 3D morphology split into hundreds or thousands of compartments, each with Hodgkin-Huxley-style channels (Na, several K, Ca, h-current, Ca-activated K). They reproduce dendritic spikes, back-propagation and the effect of where a synapse lands. Cost: about 10^3 to 10^4 equations per cell. Examples: the Hay et al. (2011) layer 5 pyramidal cell, the De Schutter and Bower (1994) Purkinje cell, Blue Brain's 207 morpho-electrical types.

Reduced compartmental models: two to a few dozen compartments that keep the key soma-dendrite interaction. The Pinsky-Rinzel (1994) two-compartment CA3 cell and two-compartment pyramidal cells with an apical calcium zone are classics. Cost: tens of equations.

Single-compartment conductance-based models: one compartment with the type's characteristic channels. The Wang-Buzsaki (1996) fast-spiking interneuron, the Pospischil et al. (2008) family of cortical and thalamic cell models, and thalamocortical cells with a T-type calcium current. Cost: 3 to 10 equations.

Adaptive integrate-and-fire models: AdEx (Brette & Gerstner 2005), Izhikevich (2003) and generalized LIF (GLIF; Mihalas & Niebur 2009, Teeter et al. 2018). Two or three variables, with parameters chosen to match the type's firing pattern, adaptation and f-I curve. Cost: 2 to 5 equations, cheap enough for networks of millions.

Plain LIF with type-specific constants: different membrane time constant, threshold, refractory period and synaptic time constants per type. The Potjans-Diesmann (2014) microcircuit uses the same LIF for all types and puts the differences into connectivity.

Rate or statistical models: a firing-rate unit, or a generalized linear model (GLM) fitted directly to spike trains (Pillow et al. 2008). These capture input-output behaviour without any membrane dynamics.

blocks.text: Rule of thumb: choose the cheapest level that still has the mechanism your question depends on. If you need dendritic gating of feedback, you need at least two compartments. If you need fast-spiking versus adapting cells, an Izhikevich or AdEx point neuron is enough. If only connectivity matters, LIF will do.
How a type-specific model is fitted

The standard recipe starts from a set of recordings of the type: responses to current steps of several amplitudes, sometimes ramps, noisy currents and hyperpolarising steps. Features are extracted from each trace (spike count, first-spike latency, adaptation index, spike height and width, after-hyperpolarisation depth, sag ratio and so on). An optimiser, usually a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm, then searches the model's free parameters (mostly maximal channel conductances) to match those features within the cell-to-cell spread of the data. Druckmann et al. (2007) introduced this feature-based approach; BluePyOpt (Van Geit et al. 2016) is the open-source tool Blue Brain uses for it, and the Allen Institute fitted its biophysical and GLIF models the same way.

For point models there are also direct fitting methods. The Allen GLIF models are fitted by linear regression on noise-driven recordings (Teeter et al. 2018). Spike-train similarity measures, such as the coincidence factor used in the INCF spike-time prediction competitions (Jolivet et al. 2008), showed that a well-fitted adaptive threshold integrate-and-fire model can predict a large share of the spikes of a real cortical neuron under noisy input (often 70 per cent or more of the spikes that the cell itself reproduces across repeated trials).

blocks.source:
Fitting a cell-type model (feature-based)

1. Collect traces:   current steps  -0.1 .. +0.5 nA, 1-2 s each
2. Extract features: spike count, ISI CV, adaptation index,
                     AP amplitude & width, AHP depth, sag ratio,
                     first-spike latency, input resistance
3. Choose a model:   morphology + channel set, or a point model
4. Free parameters:  gNa, gKdr, gKm, gCaL, gSK, gH ... per region
5. Optimise:         error_i = |model_feature_i - mean_i| / sd_i
                     minimise all error_i (multi-objective GA)
6. Validate:         on stimuli NOT used for fitting
                     (noise current, synaptic input, other cells)

items: ModelDB (senselab.med.yale.edu/modeldb): thousands of published neuron and network models with their code, searchable by cell type, channel and simulator.
Allen Cell Types Database: GLIF and all-active biophysical models fitted to individual mouse and human neurons, downloadable with the recordings they were fitted to.
Blue Brain Project / Open Brain Platform: the detailed m-type/e-type models of the rat somatosensory microcircuit and hippocampal CA1 models.
Hippocampome.org: Izhikevich parameter sets for over 100 hippocampal neuron types (Venkadesh et al. 2018), directly usable in a point-neuron network.
Open Source Brain and NeuroML-DB: models in the simulator-independent NeuroML format, which can be run in NEURON, NEST, Brian2 or jNeuroML.

Izhikevich (2003, 2004) tables: four parameters (a, b, c, d) for regular spiking, intrinsically bursting, chattering, fast spiking, low-threshold spiking, thalamocortical and resonator cells, plus his 2007 book's parameters for many specific types.

blocks.text: What this means for your SNN

items: Start with Izhikevich or AdEx parameters for each type: they are cheap, well documented and reproduce the main firing classes (see Firing Patterns, #/neuroscience/cell-types/firing-patterns).
Move a type to two compartments only when a result needs dendrites, typically the pyramidal cells that receive feedback.
Keep a detailed model of one cell around as a reference: drive it and your reduced model with the same input, and compare spike times.
Use the variability in the data. Cells of one type differ; drawing each model cell's parameters from the measured spread is more realistic than cloning one cell.
